data.description: Sediment preserving impressions left by organisms. Often a type of ichnofossil or a trace fossil. (See Donovan, S.K. (2025), The significance of traces and trace fossils: trails, burrows and borings. Geology Today, 41: 56-60. )
A type of appendage that produces lift while moving through air or some other fluid.

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=hair and appropriate modifiers. ] Also referred to as spines, these are modified hair in mammals including the prickles of hedgehogs and among rodents, the quills of both New World and Old World porcupines as well as the prickly fur of spiny mice, spiny pocket mice and spiny rats.

An anatomical structure used by mollusks for feeding, sometimes compared to a tongue.[2] It is a minutely toothed, chitinous ribbon, which is typically used for scraping or cutting food before the food enters the oesophagus.

In the vertebrate skeleton, the basal supporting structure that lies partly or wholly within the trunk and forms a stable base for the fin or limb. Use part modifiers such as pelvic or pectoral to specify if needed.
data.search_terms: innominate, ischium, pectoral girdle, pelvic girdle, pelvis, pubis, synsacrum,ilium

data.description: The chambered portion of the shell of a cephalopod. It is divided by septa into camerae.

An irregular bone in the vertebrate spinal column with a complex structure composed of bone and some hyaline cartilage, the proportions of which vary according to the segment of the backbone and the species of vertebrate.
A hard, internal structure composed primarily of aragonite in cephalopods, specifically in the family Sepiidae (cuttlefish), used for bouyancy control.
Fusion of the postorbital with the postfrontal.
A set of bones that is found in the hyoid region in most fishes, also called the hyomandibular bone.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part whole organism. ] The physical structure of a person or an animal, including the bones, flesh, and organs.

For invertebrates, typically a calcareous exoskeleton which encloses, supports and protects the soft parts of an animal in the phylum Mollusca, which includes snails, clams, cephalopods, tusk shells, and several other classes. In Arctos for phyla other than Mollusca, the appropriate part name is exoskeleton.

Mineralized, tooth-like structures from the oral cavity of conodonts. The element array constituted a feeding apparatus that is radically different from the jaws of modern animals. They are now termed "conodont elements" to avoid confusion.
A square posterior element of the cranium. In advanced therapsids, including mammals, the incus is a modified quadrate.
The curved, shelly plate from the body of an ammonite.
digital bone[ Consider using phalanx ]
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use. ] Contents of the stomach and crop.
The distal wrist bone which articulates with the ulna.
The fused caudal vertebrae of advanced birds. It is analogous to both the fused caudal vertebrae of apes, the coccyx, and the fused caudal vertebrae of frogs, the urostyle.
[ Consider using penis ]

A cranial bone found in some sarcopterygians, including some tetrapods, which connects the maxilla, squamosal, and jugal and which contacts the quadrate. The quadratojugal is reduced in primitive synapsids and entirely absent in advanced cynodonts, including mammals.

The pubis is the anterior element of the hip bone. In dinosaurs, the orientation of the pubis determines the classification of so-called 'bird-hipped' and 'lizard-hipped' or ornithischian and saurischian dinosaurs. In ornithischian dinosaurs the pubis runs backward along the ischium while in saurischian dinosaurs the pubis juts forward. Birds, which are saurischian dinosaurs, have secondarily evolved the ornithischian hip condition.

Any of various tubular organs in animals and especially mollusks or arthropods that are used for drawing in or ejecting fluids or air to be used for the purposes of locomotion, respiration, feeding, or reproduction.

Gill arches found in all chordates. In advanced chordates such as gnathostomes, pharyngeal arches migrate during embryonic development to form the maxilla and mandible. In fish, the arches are known as the branchial arches, or gill arches. Highly modified elements of the pharyngeal arches also form the ear bones of mammals.
The region of the skull that encloses the brain. Also called the neurocranium, the braincase is comprised of different bones/areas of the skull in different vertebrates.
A hard, internal structure in decapodiform and octopodiform cephalopods. Also known as a pen.

The pelvis consists of paired hipbones, connected in front at the pubic symphysis and behind by the sacrum; each is made up of three bones—the blade-shaped ilium, above and to either side, which accounts for the width of the hips; the ischium, behind and below, on which the weight falls in sitting; and the pubis, in front.
data.search_terms: ilium, innominate, ischium, pubis, synsacrum,pelvic girdle

data.description: A hole presumed to have been created by biogenic activity. A type of ichnofossil or a trace fossil. Distinguished from a burrow because a boring is destructive; individual grains in burrows are pushed aside, whereas grains are cut in place in borings. (See Donovan, S.K. (2025), The significance of traces and trace fossils: trails, burrows and borings. Geology Today, 41: 56-60.)
an anatomical structure that connects the swim bladder to the auditory system in fishes belonging to the superorder Ostariophysi

The part of an organism which usually includes the ears, brain, forehead, cheeks, chin, eyes, nose, and mouth, each of which aid in various sensory functions such as sight, hearing, smell, and taste, respectively. Some very simple animals may not have a head, but many bilaterally symmetric forms do, regardless of size.

Endochondral bone that borders that medial edge of the posttemporal fossa. The epiotics are sutured to parietals and supraoccipital dorsally, the exoccipitals ventrally and the pterotics laterally. The epiotic is a paired bone.
An unpaired bone in the skull that separates the nasal cavity from the brain. It is located at the roof of the nose, between the two orbits.
A winglike cartilaginous bone within a mammal's skull, forming part of the socket of the eye.
The nearly flat part of the shell structure of a turtle, what one would call the belly or ventral surface of the shell.
A highly vascularised organ found in some animals that houses symbiotic bacteria that provide food for their host.
A permanent projection on the head of an animals consisting of a covering of keratin and other proteins surrounding a core of live bone.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] See individual parts for definitions.
Bile, or gall, is a yellow-green fluid produced by the liver of most vertebrates that aids the digestion of lipids in the small intestines.
A bone which, in most tetrapods, is located between the clavicles.

In fishes, one of the cartilaginous or bony elements (as basalia and radialia) by which rays of the fin of a fish are supported. There may be three cartilages that ossify into proximal, median and distal pterygiophores (or axonost, mesonost and baseost or epibaseost).
Fossilized excreta. A type of ichnofossil or a trace fossil.
Contents of the ventriculus (gizzard, gigerium, or gastric mill), an organ found in the digestive tract of some animals including birds, reptiles, and some invertebrates.
The thin layer of tissue forming the natural outer covering of the body.

The rump. The sacrum is a number of fused sacral vertebrae associated with the hip. The number of vertebrae which comprise the sacrum varies from species to species. In theropod dinosaurs, including birds, the sacral vertebrae are further fused into adjoining caudal and lumbar vertebrae, as well as the hip bones, to form the synsacrum.
An ensemble of similar cells and their extracellular matrix from the same origin that together carry out a specific function.
A modified subterranean plant stem usually consisting of a relatively large, usually globe-shaped structure of modified stem and fleshy leaves that functions as food storage organs during dormancy.

Microscopic amorphous bio-silica structures that are produced within and between plant cells by precipitation and polymerization of silica. Often preserved in plant tissue or preserved in sedimentary rocks as part of the fossil record.
The bone that surrounds the inner ear of birds and mammals, formed from the fusion of the prootic, epiotic, and opisthotic.

A bony external plate or scale overlaid with horn, as on the shell of a turtle, the skin of crocodilians, and the feet of birds. If the horn or keratinous layer is not present, the appropriate part name is osteoderm along with the part modifier scute, bony. If both the keratinous and bony parts of the scute are present, it will be advantageous to record two parts, scute and osteoderm. The term is also used to describe the anterior portion of the mesonotum in insects as well as some arachnids (e.g., the family Ixodidae, the scale ticks).
A calcified structure located at the base of the siphons in bivalve mollusks of the family Teredinidae used to seal the burrow entrance.

An organ of the visual system. Eyes provide animals with vision, the ability to receive and process visual detail, as well as enabling several photo response functions that are independent of vision. Eyes detect light and convert it into electro-chemical impulses in neurons.

This term is used to describe a hard chitinous or calcareous plate, piece, scale, spine, or spicule, most typically associated corals, echinoderms, mollusks, and regions of the arthropod integument. It may be: a) Hard chitinous structure, typically associated with regions of the arthropod integument. In arthropods, these hardened plates are formed through a process known as sclerotization, which strengthens and rigidifies the chitin-protein matrix, contributing to the exoskeleton's durability and protection; b) a calcareous structure of several forms present in most octocorals species. In octocorals, the sclerites are produced by specialized cells and consist of polycrystalline aggregates of calcite deposited over a fibrous matrix. Their shape, size, and coloration can vary widely among species, playing a role in their structural support and protection. Taxonomy of octocorals relies on sclerites as diagnostic morphological characters; c) a calcareous scale or spine present on the bodies of aculiferan molluscs (aplacophorans and chitons). Their shape, size, and whether or not they are hollow vary among species and is taxonomically informative.
The uppermost and largest part of the hip bone.
The bone that forms the lower jaw and holds the lower teeth in place. Also called lower jaw or jawbone.In arthropods, a pair of mouthparts used either for biting or cutting and holding food.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] See individual parts for definitions.
a female reproductive organ in which ova or eggs are produced
A curved element of the axial skeleton which extends down from the vertebra or up from the sternum, enclosing the body cavity, found in almost all vertebrates.
In fungi, the structure on which sporangia (spore-producing structures) are borne.
A structure built for certain animals to hold eggs, offspring, and, oftentimes, the animal itself.
An anatomical structure which is the terminal portion of a limb which bears weight and allows locomotion, or an invertebrate organ of locomotion or attachment.
A long bone in the arm that runs from the shoulder to the elbow.
A device manufactured or created to position, display or support an object.
The gizzard, gigerium, or gastric mill, is an organ found in the digestive tract of some animals including birds, reptiles, and some invertebrates.

A limb of an animal used especially for supporting the body and for walking. A pole or bar serving as a support or prop . The part of the upper (as of a boot) that extends above the ankle.[ Consider using limb ]
The two bones in the skull which, when joined together at a fibrous joint, form the sides and roof of the cranium.
Hard translucent fossilized resin produced by coniferous trees, typically yellowish in color.

Cells that (a) have been isolated from living tissue or (b) are the cultured progeny of free-living unicellular or multicellular organism(s), which can subsequently be maintained under carefully controlled conditions.

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer a specific part name and appropriate modifiers. ] A fossil formed when an animal, plant, or other organism dies, its flesh decays and bones deteriorate due to chemical reactions; minerals gradually enter into the cavity, resulting in a cast, also called a mold fossil, which is in the general form of the original organism.
Extensions of the skull often grown by members of the deer family; also used for antilocaprids
or small bowel is an organ in the gastrointestinal tract where most of the absorption of nutrients and minerals from food takes place. It lies between the stomach and large intestine.
The fused bones of the frontal and parietal in amphibians. (See Rocek, Z. (1988). Origin and evolution of the frontoparietal complex in anurans. Amphibia-Reptilia, 9(4), 385-403.)
The scroll-like, curved bone structure located within the nasal cavity of vertebrates.

Deoxyribonucleic acid, a molecule composed of two polynucleotide chains that coil around each other to form a double helix carrying genetic instructions for the development, functioning, growth and reproduction of all known organisms and many viruses.
The reddish-brown bean-shaped organ that receives blood from the paired renal arteries.
The posterior part of the body of an arthropod, especially the segments of an insect's body behind the thorax.

The tympanic part of the temporal bone is a curved plate of bone lying below the squamous part of the temporal bone, in front of the mastoid process, and surrounding the external part of the ear canal.
An internal support structure of an animal, composed of mineralized tissue.
Each of the upper and lower bony structures in vertebrates forming the framework of the mouth and containing the teeth.[ Consider using mandible and maxilla ]

Bones of the wrist located between the metacarpals (finger bones) and the radius and ulna. Carpals form the second 'elbow' joint in digitigrade and unguligrade tetrapods. Present in all sarcopterygian fishes, including tetrapods.

A form of stromatolite, which grow on rocks and are often found rolling loose in the sediments at certain times of year. They occur in water up to 1 m deep, and are primarily formed laminated algal hemispheres of Phormidium hendersonii.
The biological system made up of all the anatomical organs involved in sexual reproduction.
The posterior body part or shield of crustaceans and some other arthropods, such as insects and the extinct trilobites.

The tail is the section at the rear end of certain kinds of animals’ bodies; in general, the term refers to a distinct, flexible appendage to the torso. It is the part of the body that corresponds roughly to the sacrum and coccyx in mammals, reptiles, and birds; for fish, the area between the anterior end of the anal fin to the anterior end of the caudal fin . While tails are primarily a feature of vertebrates, some invertebrates including scorpions and springtails, as well as snails and slugs, have tail-like appendages that are sometimes referred to as tails.
An organ found in all vertebrates. Similar in structure to a large lymph node, it acts primarily as a blood filter.
Contents of the crop.
A solid, waxy, flammable substance of a dull grey or blackish colour produced in the digestive system of sperm whales.

Bones of the ankle located between the metatarsals (foot bones) and the fibula and tibia (lower hindlimb bones). Tarsals form the second 'knee' joint in digitigrade and unguligrade tetrapods. Present in all sarcopterygian fishes, including tetrapods. These bones are also known as the tarsus collectively.
The bone below the operculum in the opercular series in fish.
The kneecap. It is found in mammals, birds, and frogs.
Paired appendages used for sensing in arthropods.
The fat of sea mammals, especially whales and seals.
The complete set of chromosomes in a species or in an individual organism.
A bone of the lower jaw in some tetrapods, anterior to the articular and above the angular bones.
The three most proximal tarsals, so named because of their wedge-like shape.
A bone of the mandible connected to all other jaw bones. In advanced therapsids, including mammals, the tympanic bone is a modified angular.

A enclosed cavity presumed to have been created by biogenic activity. A type of ichnofossil or a trace fossil. Distinguished from a boring because a boring is destructive; individual grains in burrows are pushed aside, whereas grains are cut in place in borings. (See Donovan, S.K. (2025), The significance of traces and trace fossils: trails, burrows and borings. Geology Today, 41: 56-60.)
A muscular organ in animals which pumps blood through the blood vessels of the circulatory system

A bone structure that forms the head in vertebrates. It supports the structures of the face and provides a protective cavity for the brain. The skull is composed of two parts: the cranium and the mandible.
The heel bone in non-human therian mammals. In humans the same bone is called the calcaneus.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] See individual parts for definitions.
Ribonucleic acid is a polymeric molecule essential in various biological roles in coding, decoding, regulation and expression of genes.
An appendage, typically made of keratin, found at the end of a toe or finger in most amniotes.
The organic vessel containing the zygote in which an embryo develops until it can survive on its own, at which point the animal hatches.

The triangular arch of bone which protrudes from the base of a vertebra. It is fused to the centrum or absent in most mammals. The chevron, also sometimes called the haemal arch, is the ventral counterpart of the neural arch.

Of or pertaining to the nose, as a nasal bone (paired) on the dorsal surface of the skull at its anterior end. A nasal bone.The paired nasal is the frontmost bone of the skull roof, and the largest bone of the top surface of the snout. It is situated between the premaxilla in front and the frontal behind.
A permanent projection on the head of an animals consisting of a core of bone that was once surrounded by a sheath of keratin and other proteins.

The round central element of a vertebra. The spinal cord runs between the centrum and the neural arch through a cylindrical cavity called the neural canal. The centrum is more or less fused to other vertebral elements in various vertebrates.
Dietary remains taken from cheek of individual.
The cranial bone which forms the posterior rim of the orbital and connects to the frontal and squamosal bone in some archosaurs.

The tract from the mouth to the anus which includes all the organs of the digestive system in humans and other animals. Also called GI tract, GIT, digestive tract, digestion tract, or alimentary canal.

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=skin and appropriate modifiers. ] A pocketlike fold of skin in the cheeks of various animals, such as squirrels, gophers, and monkeys, that functions as a means of carrying food.
A horseshoe-shaped bone situated in the anterior midline of the neck between the chin and the thyroid cartilage.
The bone which forms the distal ridge of the eye socket. In mammals the same bone is called the zygomatic.
A temporary fetal organ that begins developing from the blastocyst shortly after implantation.
The posterior element of the hip bone.
Placeholder generic part name for cultural objects; likely to change when and if we can disentangle parts and taxonomy.

A body fluid in animals that delivers necessary substances such as nutrients and oxygen to the cells and transports metabolic waste products away from those same cells. In vertebrates, it is composed of blood cells suspended in blood plasma.
An organ of the digestive system and endocrine system of vertebrates.
Adipose tissue, body fat, or simply fat is a loose connective tissue composed mostly of adipocytes.
The external sex organs.
A sheet of internal skeletal muscle in humans and other mammals that extends across the bottom of the thoracic cavity.
The proximal bone of the hind limb of vertebrates.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] NO DESCRIPTION DO NOT USE
Baleen is a filter-feeding system inside the mouths of baleen whales.
The most distal tarsal bone.
A structure at the distal end of the penis in male mammals. Commonly referred to as the glans.
Also womb, a major female hormone-responsive secondary sex organ of the reproductive system in humans and most other mammals.
The collarbones which connect the shoulder blade to the sternum. In theropod dinosaurs (including birds) the clavicles are fused to form the furcula, or wishbone.
A bone associated with the scapula in some tetrapods. The coracoid process found in therian is similar in appearance but non-homologous.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part skin and appropriate modifiers. ] Consider using skin with toe pad as remark or attribute.
Part captured by flushing nasal passage (e.g., looking for nasal mites).
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] See individual parts for definitions.
The combination or fusion of the three hip bones; the pubis, ischium, and ilium.
data.search_terms: ilium, ischium, pelvis, pubis, synsacrum,pelvic girdle

data.description: A hollow muscular organ in humans and other vertebrates that stores urine from the kidneys before disposal by urination.
Any of the pieces of hard whitish tissue making up the skeleton in humans and other vertebrates; including paleontological, zoological, or archaeological samples.
a cranial dermal bone and the main bone of the occiput (back and lower part of the skull)
Also called brown adipose tissue, is a special type of body fat that is turned on (activated) when an organism is cold.
A mixed gland that produces the gametes (sex cells) and sex hormones of an organism.
Everything but the shell.

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, catalog separately. ] A phylum of parasitic worms that have an elongate sac-like body, no internal alimentary canal, and use a spiny protrusible proboscis for attachment to the intestinal wall.

The segment of the gastrointestinal tract extending from the pyloric sphincter of the stomach to the anus and as in other mammals, consists of two segments, the small intestine and the large intestine. [ If entire gastrointestinal tract is preserved, use "gastrointestinal tract" as part name. ]

The bones of the upper jaw. In primitive gnathostomes such as sharks the maxilla is separate from the cranium (the braincase). The maxilla is articulated with the cranium in intermediate gnathostomes such as osteichthians and primitive tetrapods. In advanced gnathostomes, such as birds and mammals, the maxilla is fused to the cranium.

Environmental samples include air, water, soil, dust, biological materials and wastes (liquids, solids or sludges) collected for the purpose of analysis of microbial communities, pathogens, eDNA, toxins, pollutants, etc.
Upper portion of the skull that includes the facial bones, cranial bones, and braincase and that does not include the mandible (when present in the organism).

Mouthpart(s) are highly specialized oral structures adapted for diverse feeding habits, especially in insects, fish and larval amphibians. For example, in larval anurans, they primarily consist of keratinized jaw sheaths, tooth ridges (keratodonts), and papillae, forming an oral disc used for scraping algae or filtering food from water, or for locomotion.
A term for any beak-like structure, analogous of which may be found throughout the animal kingdom.

In animals, a gland is a group of cells in an animal's body that synthesizes substances (such as hormones) for release into the bloodstream or into cavities inside the body or its outer surface.In plants, a gland is defined functionally as a plant structure which secretes one or more products. This may be located on or near the plant surface and secrete externally, or be internal to the plant and secrete into a canal or reservoir.
A muscular organ in the mouth of a typical vertebrate. It manipulates food for mastication and swallowing as part of the digestive process, and is the primary organ of taste.
The smaller counterpart of the radius located in the lower forelimb. It is fused to the radius in some ungulates and amphibians.
Testicle or testis (plural testes) is the male reproductive gland or gonad in all animals.
The breastplate, a bone which is connected to and suspended by the false (ventral) ribs. In advanced birds, the sternum is keeled to allow for the attachment of large flight muscles.
No description of the part is available.
of, relating to, or constituting a bone between the prootic and epiotic in the dorsal and outer part of the periotic capsule

A muscular, hollow organ in the gastrointestinal tract of humans and many other animals, including several invertebrates. The stomach has a dilated structure and functions as a vital digestive organ. It performs a chemical breakdown by means of enzymes and hydrochloric acid.
Also known as the windpipe, a cartilaginous tube that connects the larynx to the bronchi of the lungs, allowing the passage of air, and so is present in almost all air-breathing animals with lungs.
Blood serum is the fluid and solute component of blood which does not play a role in clotting.
A protein filament that grows from follicles found in the dermis. Hair is one of the defining characteristics of mammals.
Paired cranial bone found in many tetrapods that connected the pterygoid bone to the outer surface of the braincase.
One of the appendages of some echinoderms that branch off the central calyx or disk and are used for movement or feeding.
A contiguous alive or once living physical entity; entity or being that is or was living; an individual living or once living thing, such as one animal, plant, fungus, or bacterium.
The solid or semi-solid remains of food that was not digested in the small intestine, and has been broken down by bacteria in the large intestine. Intestinal excrement, droppings, scat.

A jointed, muscled appendage of a tetrapod vertebrate animal used for weight-bearing, terrestrial locomotion and physical interaction with other objects. Use part modifiers such as fore, hind, anterior, or posterior to specify position.
A hard, calcified structure found in the jaws (or mouths) of many vertebrates and used to break down food.
A bone found in the penis of many placental mammals.
An external anatomical structure of birds that is used for eating and for preening, manipulating objects, killing prey, fighting for food, courtship and feeding young.
Dietary remains taken from bill of individual.
Bone that is ventral, median, and associated with branchial arch 1 (pharyngeal arch 3). Typically develops in the anterior copula cartilage.
A posterior cranial element which connects the jugal (or zygomatic) to the postorbital (or parietal in mammals).

The bone which forms the posterior portion of the palate (the roof of the mouth) in advanced synapsids. The same bone has convergently evolved in archosaurs to extend the palate in a similar way. In more basal gnathostomes, the palatine bones are separate within the maxilla.
Relating to or being a bone in the base of the cranium immediately in front of the foramen magnum.
The bone in the ankle that articulates with the leg bones to form the ankle joint.
A hollow, bony prominence of rounded form (in most mammals formed by the tympanic bone) partly enclosing structures of the middle and inner ear.

For serological studies, blood clots are obtained from clotted blood that has not been mixed with an anticoagulant which may be centrifuged to separate out and collect serum. The blood serum is typically collected in mottled red/gray, gold, or cherry red-top tubes, and red-top (gel barrier) tubes which contain clot activator and gel for separating serum from cells, but not anticoagulant. Serum may be removed, and the residual clot may be preserved separately and frozen.
Liquid component of blood in which blood cells are absent, but which contains proteins and other constituents of whole blood in suspension.
A tooth-bearing bone of the lower jaw. In mammals, it is the only bone on a side; in all other vertebrates, it is accompanied by other bones.
Paired (or fused) cranial bone in many tetrapods found behind the parietal, forming the back of the skull.
An organ of soft nervous tissue contained in the skull of vertebrates, functioning as the coordinating center of sensation and intellectual and nervous activity.
A bone of the mandible. In advanced therapsids (including mammals) the malleus is a modified articular.
Paired cranial bone found in many tetrapods that is part of the skull roof, between and behind the eye orbits, lateral to the frontal and parietal bones, and anterior to the postorbital bone.

Relating to or being the part of the base of the cranium that lies between the basioccipital and the presphenoid bones and that usually ossifies separately and becomes a part of the sphenoid bone only in the adult.
A small rigid plate that grows out of an animal's skin.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=unknown and remarks. ] Unspecified parts of an organism, unknown preservation/preparation.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] See individual parts for definitions.
A semi-solid tissue found within the spongy or cancellous portions of bones.
A woody structural member connected to but not part of the central trunk of a tree or a shrub.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=skin and appropriate modifiers. ] A cape is an animal hide from the nose to just behind the front shoulders.
Dorsal part of the turtle shell or the exoskeleton over the cephalothorax of an arthropod.
A large blister containing serous fluid.

In plants, the outermost whorl of parts that form a flower. The body disk that is covered with a leathery tegumen containing calcareous plates (in crinoids and ophiuroids the main part of the body where the viscera are located). The spicules containing the basal portion of the upper tentacular part of the polyp of some soft corals (also called calice). A body part of the Entoprocta from which tentacles arise and the mouth and anus are located.
A patch of featherless skin on the underside of birds during the nesting season.
A pouch within the peritoneum that is considered to be the beginning of the large intestine.
A tube formed by the calcareous secretions of certain invertebrates.
An undeveloped or embryonic shoot and normally occurs in the axil of a leaf or at the tip of a stem.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=whole organism and modifiers. ]The decaying flesh of dead animals, including human flesh.
A mace-like spiny-headed rod found on the mid-dorsal surface of heads of male Holocephali. Thought to aid in holding the female during copulation.
The firm, whitish, flexible connective tissue found in various forms in the larynx and respiratory tract, in structures such as the external ear, and in the articulating surfaces of joints.
The fused carpal and metacarpal bones found in the wings of advanced birds. Primitive birds lack this and retain fingers.
Also named claw, nipper, or pincer, is a pincer-like organ terminating certain limbs of some arthropods.
The head section of an arthropod.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, catalog separately. ] Cestodes
An organ on plants in the division Pinophyta (conifers) that contains the reproductive structures.
Concretions formed when peat is turned to stone via the precipitation of calcite. Paradoxically, coal balls are not made of coal.
A thin-walled expanded portion of the alimentary tract used for the storage of food prior to digestion. Also called a croup or a craw, ingluvies, or sublingual pouch.
The skeleton of a solitary coral or a coral colony (plural = coralla). An individual within a colony is called a corallite.
A thin-walled, hollow organ or cavity containing a liquid secretion.

a large bone that extends upwards from the base of the pectoral fin and anchors to the cranium above the gills, forming the posterior edge of the gill chamber. The bone has scientific use as a means to determine the age of fishes.
Small bumps on a tooth that serve to give the tooth a serrated edge. Also called serrations. A small tooth or toothlike projection.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, catalog separately. ] External parasites.
unspecified bone from the ear
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=skin and appropriate modifiers. ] A clip of the organ of hearing and, in mammals, balance.
An anterior element of the palatoquadrate in amphibians and primitive amniotes. In mammals, the ectopterygoid is fused with the pterygoid and much reduced to form the pterygoid process.
The organ of hearing and, in mammals, balance.

The electric organ is an organ that an electric fish uses to create an electric field. Electric organs are derived from modified muscle or in some cases nerve tissue, and have evolved at least six times among the elasmobranchs and teleosts.
An egg case or egg capsule is the protective casing that surrounds the eggs of oviparous sharks, skates, chimaeras, and some gastropods and cephalopods.

The membrane which encloses the amniotic fluid of amniote eggs. In some cases the shell is proteinaceous, in others it is mineralized by calcite. The outer covering of a hard-shelled egg and of some forms of eggs with soft outer coats.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part whole organism. ] The early stage of development of a multicellular organism.
The remains of an exoskeleton and related structures that are left after ecdysozoans (including insects, crustaceans and arachnids) have moulted.
Sections of cranial bone which flank the foramen magnum, including the proximal edges of the occipital condyles.

The external skeleton that supports and protects an animal's body, in contrast to the internal skeleton (endoskeleton) of, for example, a human. In Arctos, exoskeletons of the phylum Mollusca are referred to as "shell", for all other phyla use "exoskeleton".
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, catalog separately. ] Internal parasites.
Epidermal growths that form a distinctive outer covering, or plumage, on dinosaurs, both avian (bird) and some non-avian (non-bird) and possibly other archosauromorphs.
Sometimes known as a bloom or blossom, is the reproductive structure found in flowering plants (plants of the division Magnoliophyta, also called angiosperms).

The most distinctive anatomical features of a fish. They are composed of bony spines or rays protruding from the body with skin covering them and joining them together, either in a webbed fashion, as seen in most bony fish, or similar to a flipper, as seen in sharks.

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=fin and remarks. ] A clip of the most distinctive anatomical features of a fish. They are composed of bony spines or rays protruding from the body with skin covering them and joining them together, either in a webbed fashion, as seen in most bony fish, or similar to a flipper, as seen in sharks.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part whole organism. ] The unborn offspring of an animal that develops from an embryo.
A semi-permeable paper barrier placed perpendicular to a liquid or air flow. It is used to separate fine substances from liquids or air.
A broad, flattened limb adapted for aquatic locomotion.
The calf bone, the smaller counterpart of the tibia located in the lower hindlimb. It is fused to the tibia in some ungulates and theropod dinosaurs.
A sample of material from the Earth's crust.
The seed-bearing structure in flowering plants (also known as angiosperms) formed from the ovary after flowering.
A cranial bone which forms the forehead in mammals and dinosaurs. It is more posteriorly located and reduced in other vertebrates.

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer descriptive part and modifiers. ] Any preserved evidence of life from a past geological age, such as the impressions and remains of organisms embedded in stratified rocks. (2) The mineralized remains of an animal or plant. adjective. Having the characteristic, or pertaining to the nature, of a fossil.
growth on the external tissues of plants, fungi, or animals caused by various parasites, viruses, fungi, bacteria, insects, or mites.
Dermal bones found in the ventral body wall of modern crocodilian and Sphenodon species as well as a variety of extinct animals.
The wishbone, formed from fused clavicle bones. It is found in certain theropod dinosaurs, including birds.

Also called a stomach stone or gizzard stone, is a rock held inside a gastrointestinal tract. Gastroliths in some species are retained in the muscular gizzard and used to grind food in animals lacking suitable grinding teeth. In other species the rocks are ingested and pass through the digestive system and are frequently replaced.
A respiratory organ found in many aquatic organisms that extracts dissolved oxygen from water and excretes carbon dioxide.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] mixed tissue, recommend not using
The apical portion of the shell of belemnoids, also called rostrum.

One of two cranial bones which flanks the foramen magnum (the hole connecting the vertebral column to the brain stem) and which connects to the atlas, the first vertebra in the spine.
A pair of intromittent organs of male squamates (snakes, lizards and worm lizards). [ Consider changing to the singular ]
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] heart, liver, lung, muscle tissue samples, combined in same container

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] The muscular organ in animals which pumps blood through the blood vessels of the circulatory system; the organ found only in vertebrates which detoxifies various metabolites, synthesizes proteins, and produces biochemicals necessary for digestion; and a sample of muscle tissue. The organs may be whole or sample tissues.

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] The muscular organ in animals which pumps blood through the blood vessels of the circulatory system and the organ found only in vertebrates which detoxifies various metabolites, synthesizes proteins, and produces biochemicals necessary for digestion. May be the entire organs or sample tissues.
Content of the posterior (caudal) part of the alimentary canal. Also called or epigaster.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] See individual parts for definitions.

The hard exterior portion of the hoof.
The anvil, the middle ear bones in advanced therapsids, derived from a mandibular element called the quadrate bone in other gnathostomes.

The bony structure (often fan-shaped) that chiefly is composed of the expanded, flattened and partially fused hemal spines (ventral extensions of the vertebrae), and that supports the caudal-fin rays in most bony fishes; when counting vertebrae, this composite element is treated as a single vertebra and included in the count.
A dermal bone situated between the parietal and supraoccipital. It is homologous to the postparietal bones of other animals.
The median of the three elements composing the centra of the vertebrae in some fossil batrachians.

The part of the vertebrate skeletal, typically in amphibians and reptiles, that supports the muscles of the tongue or buccal cavity and consists of four visceral arches - the hyoid arch (most cranial) and the first three branchial (pharyngeal) arches or its homologues, and may include: basibranchial, basihyal, ceratohyal, ceratobranchial, urohyal and hyobranchial elements. These component structures may or may not be ossified.

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] See individual parts for definitions.

A small proximal element of the eye socket in mammals. It forms a larger portion of the eye socket and part of the nostril in more primitive sarcopterygians, such as lungfish and basal amphibians. The lacrimal forms the posterior region of the antorbital fenestra in theropod dinosaurs.

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] The large intestine, also known as the colon or large bowel, is the last part of the gastrointestinal tract and of the digestive system in vertebrates. This part should be used for a large intestine sample containing feces without designating preservation method in the part name.
The large intestine, also known as the colon or large bowel, is the last part of the gastrointestinal tract and of the digestive system in vertebrates.

A wing-like bone of the anterior part of the lateral wall of the braincase. Not visible from the outside, it is located anterior to the prootic and contacts the parietal, frontal, and postorbital above. The laterosphenoid as a distinct ossification is unique to archosauriforms; in other reptiles this part of the neurocranial cartilage does not ossify.
The primary photosynthetic organs of vascular plants.
The organ found only in vertebrates which detoxifies various metabolites, synthesizes proteins, and produces biochemicals necessary for digestion.
An organ in the top of the neck involved in breathing, producing sound and protecting the trachea against food aspiration.
An organ of the lymphatic system.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] See individual parts for definitions.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] mixed
The hammer, one of the ear bones in advanced therapsids, derived from a mandibular element called the articular in other gnathostomes.
The primary organ of the respiratory system in many animals including a few fish and some snails.
A small diploid cell which, upon maturation, forms a primordial follicle in a female fetus or the female (haploid or diploid) gametangium of certain thallophytes.
The crescent-shaped carpal bone found in-between the other proximal carpals.
Also known as the capitate. The largest carpal bone located in the center of the wrist.
The cheekbone, the bone which forms the ventral distal rim of the eye socket. Also called the zygomatic bone, it is the mammalian equivalent of the jugal.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] See individual parts for definitions.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] See individual parts for definitions.
Designating or pertaining to the mastoid bone (paired) or its process. This bone is bounded by the squamosal bone, the exoccipital bone, and the tympanic bone.
The hand, the terminal element of the forelimb in tetrapods.
The dorsal body wall which covers the visceral mass and usually protrudes in the form of flaps well beyond the visceral mass itself. Also known by the Latin word pallium.
Photographs, literature, field notes, or digital media devices.

Of or pertaining to a metacarpal bone. A bone of the hand or forefoot between the wrist and fingers; when all the digits are present ,there are five more or less elongated metacarpal bones, one at the base of each digit.
The bones which connect the ankle bones to the digits. The metatarsals form the third segment of the hindlimb in digitigrade and unguligrade tetrapods.
Soft tissue found in most animals which contains protein filaments of actin and myosin.

A solid piece of debris from an object, such as a comet, asteroid, or meteoroid, that originated in outer space and survived its passage through the atmosphere to reach the surface of a planet or moon.

a multi-layered sheet of microorganisms, mainly bacteria and archaea, and also just bacterial. Microbial mats grow at interfaces between different types of material, mostly on submerged or moist surfaces, but a few survive in deserts.
An informative representation of an object, person or system. May or may not be at scale.

The bones of the hand or foot which connect the wrist or ankle bones to the digits. Metapodials are referred to as metacarpals in forelimbs and metatarsals in hindlimbs. The metapodials form the third segment of the leg in digitigrade and unguligrade tetrapods.

The triangular arch of bone which protrudes from the top of a vertebra. It is fused to the centrum in most mammals. The spinal cord runs between the centrum and the neural arch through a cylindrical cavity called the neural canal. The neural arch is the dorsal counterpart of the haemal arch or chevron.
The proximal tarsal located between the posterior proximal tarsal (the talus) and the anterior proximal tarsals (the cuneiform bones).
The fusion of the navicular and cuboid bones found in some ungulates.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, catalog separately. ] Nematode.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] mixed tissue, recommend not using

When the spinous process of the neural arch exceeds the length of the transverse process, it is called a neural spine. Neural spines form the sails of animals such as Dimetrodon and Spinosaurus, as well as the humps of animals such as bison or muskoxen.
A spindle of bone, often a mineralized ligament.

A corneous or calcareous anatomical structure like a trapdoor which exists in many (but not all) groups of sea snails and freshwater snails, and also in a few groups of land snails and some marine and freshwater gastropods. A series of bones found in bony fish and chimaeras that serves as a facial support structure and a protective covering for the gills of fish. A membraneous, horny or cartilaginous flap that covers the nares of some birds. In the bryozoan order Cheilostomatida, a calcareous or chitinous lid-like structure that protects the opening through which the polypide protrudes.
A calcium carbonate structure in the saccule or utricle of the inner ear, specifically in the vestibular system of vertebrates. Also called statoconium or otoconium or statolith.

Bone deposits found in the skin, including bone scales, scutes, ridges, and plates. If the horn or keratinous layer is also present, the appropriate part name is scute. If both the keratinous and bony parts of the scute are present, it will be advantageous to record two parts, scute and osteoderm.
The roof of the mouth, consisting of the structures that separate the mouth from the nasal cavity. The bony palate is composed of the following bones: premaxillae, maxillae, and palatines.
A bone inside the clitoris of many mammalian taxa. It is homologous to the baculum in male mammals.
A hard, glistening object produced within the soft tissue (specifically the mantle) of a living shelled mollusk or another animal, such as fossil conulariids.
A mass of undigested parts of a bird's food that some bird species occasionally regurgitate.
The most proximal wrist bone which connects to the radius.
bone which can be found in the cranium of many vertebrates. It is an unpaired dermal bone which lies at the midline of the roof of the mouth.
The primary sexual organ that male animals use to inseminate females (or hermaphrodites) during copulation.
A membrane that covers the outer surface of all bones,[1] except at the articular surfaces (i.e. the parts within a joint space) of long bones.
Unspecified bones of the wrist and ankle. In digitigrade and unguligrade animals the podials form the second joint in the limb after the elbow or knee.
The foot, the terminal element of the hindlimb in tetrapods. [ Consider using foot ]
Pereiopods are primarily walking legs and are also used for gathering food. They are also the ten legs from which decapods take their name.
A bone in a finger distal to the metacarpus or in a toe distal to the metatarsus. Digital bones in the hands and feet of most vertebrates.
A fine to coarse powdery substance comprising pollen grains which are male microgametophytes of seed plants, which produce male gametes (sperm cells).

The basal element of the temporal. Part of the inner ear canal. The petrous part of the temporal bone is pyramid-shaped and is wedged in at the base of the skull between the sphenoid and occipital bones.
A bone peculiar to the ornithischian dinosaurs, an unpaired beak-like bone which protrudes from the anterior tip of the dentary.
One of three cranial bones which enclose the inner ear in primitive tetrapods. It is fused with the epiotic and opisthotic bones in mammals to form the periotic bone.
The bone which forms the back of the palate in many vertebrates.
The fusion of the radius and ulna in the forelimbs of amphibians.
The fingerlike projections located near the junction of the stomach and the intestine. Also as pyloric ceca.
One of a pair of small cranial bones at the very tip of the upper jaw of many animals, usually, but not always, bearing teeth.
The larger counterpart of the ulna located in the lower forelimb. It is fused to the ulna in some ungulates and amphibians.
The bone between the cheek and the gill cover.

The cranial bone joined to the lacrimal and frontal bone within the skulls of sarcopterygian fishes, including tetrapods. It is absent in advanced therapsids and theropod dinosaurs, though it is prominent in both primitive dinosaurs and synapsids.
The organs of a plant that are modified to provide anchorage for the plant and take in water and nutrients into the plant body.
Root systems that have been encased in mineral matter.Rhizoliths are created through processes of chemical weathering, decomposition, reprecipitation and cementation.
A modified subterranean plant stem that sends out roots and shoots from its nodes.
Any naturally occurring solid mass or aggregate of minerals or mineraloid matter.

A component of a ring of bone which encircles the pupil. Sclerotic rings are present in many groups of vertebrates, though they are not ubiquitous in any class. Modern mammals and crocodilians entirely lack sclerotic rings.
An embryonic plant enclosed in a protective outer covering.

A substance which accumulates through the laying down of material over time. Clastic sediments are formed when chunks entrained in a fluid, usually air or water, loose energy and settle out of the flow. Chemical sediments are formed when changes in solubility cause dissolved chemicals to precipitate out of a liquid, usually water.
The combination of the coracoid and scapula found in many vertebrates. Therian mammals, which lack the coracoid, do not possess a scapulocoracoid.
The shoulder blade, the bone which connects the humerus to the clavicle.

A dry specimen is usually mounted on a specimen stub using an adhesive such as epoxy resin or electrically conductive double-sided adhesive tape, and sputter-coated with gold or gold/palladium alloy before examination in a scanning electron microscope.
part of an incomplete skeleton for which a count of the bones is not feasible
Any bone which is suspended in tendons or muscles.
structural (skeletal) element of sponges created by the meshing together of spicules
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=skin and appropriate modifiers. ] Consider using skin with appropriate preservation modifiers.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=skin and appropriate modifiers. ] Skin that is stuffed but missing the head, possibly also missing at least one wing and leg. Possibly the same as a schmoo.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=skin and appropriate modifiers. ] A skin preparation that conserves the entire skull of a bird. Like a "schmoo"?
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=skin and appropriate modifiers. ] Naturally-shed skin.

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=skin and appropriate modifiers. ] Skin that is stuffed but may be boneless, may have one measurable leg and wing left, or may have bill cut off just inside the skin; specialized type of bird preparation that is typically accompanied by preservation of a complete skeleton in addition to the skin. See Robert W. Dickerman, 1989, "Schmoo Preparation" in "Notes from a Workshop on Bird Specimen Preparation held at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in Conjunction with the 107th Stated Meeting of the American Ornithologists' Union" (compiled by Stephen P. Rogers and D. Scott Wood).

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=skin and appropriate modifiers. ] Skin (including feathers, hair, scales) that is removed from the body, pinned flat and dried rather than stuffed with cotton.

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=skin and appropriate modifiers. ] Skin (including feathers, hair, scales) that is removed from the body and stuffed with cotton or similar inert material, preserved by drying (often in a linear position to conserve storage space, in contrast to a mount).
The fusion of the sacral vertebrae, hip bones, as well as nearby caudal and lumbar vertebrae. A bone found in theropod dinosaurs, including birds.

data.description: [ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=skin and appropriate modifiers. ] Thin layer of tissue forming the natural outer covering of the body, chemically preserved.

In a zoological context, spines are hard, needle-like anatomical structures found in both vertebrate and invertebrate species. The spines of most spiny mammals are modified hairs, with a spongy center covered in a thick, hard layer of keratin and a sharp, sometimes barbed tip.

A compound bone that forms the base of the cranium, behind the eye and below the front part of the brain. It has two pairs of broad lateral “wings” and a number of other projections, and contains two air-filled sinuses.
The fusion of the sphenoid and ethmoid bones found in some amphibians.
The male reproductive cell, or gamete, in anisogamous forms of sexual reproduction.
Also called the stirrup, a middle ear bone present in all tetrapods. It is homologous to the hyomandibula found in teleostomi.

One of two main structural axes of a vascular plant, the other being the root. It supports leaves, flowers and fruits, transports water and dissolved substances between the roots and the shoots in the xylem and phloem, stores nutrients, and produces new living tissue.
A unit of sexual or asexual reproduction that may be adapted for dispersal and for survival, often for extended periods of time, in unfavourable conditions.
A small proximal (lingual) element of the mandible which is absent in mammals.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] NO DESCRIPTION DO NOT USE
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer part=tissue and remarks. ] See individual parts for definitions.
The element of a crinoid that extends from the base of the calyx and anchors the crinoid to the sea floor. The individual skeletal elements of the stalk are called columnals.
Contents of the stomach.
A strobilating section of a helminth. Strobilisation or transverse fission is a form of asexual reproduction consisting of the spontaneous transverse segmentation of the body.

[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use. ] Material found in the stomach plus material found in the crop of a bird or invertebrate, may include the organs and lining or just the material removed from them during prep.
Layered sedimentary formations that are created by photosynthetic cyanobacteria.

The suprangular or surangular is a jaw bone found in most land vertebrates, except mammals. Usually in the back of the jaw, on the upper edge, it is connected to all other jaw bones: dentary, angular, splenial and articular.
A bone on the dorsal side of the great foramen of the skull, usually forming a part of the occipital in the adult, but distinct in the young.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use. ]A muscular, hollow organ in the gastrointestinal tract of humans and many other animals, including several invertebrates. Includes the contents.
A cranial element which connects the parietal and squamosal together.
An absorbent pad or piece of material. Should be accompanied by part attribute(s) specifying where and how the swab was used.
One of a pair of triangular flat bones along the rear edge of the skull which form pointed structures known as tabular horns in primitive Teleostomi.
A complex vocal organ found in some birds, analogous to mammalian vocal folds in function but not in form. Some elements of the syrinx are mineralized.
A test is the hard shell of some spherical marine animals, notably sea urchins and microorganisms such as testate foraminiferans, radiolarians, and testate amoebae.
The temporal bones are situated at the sides and base of the skull, and lateral to the temporal lobes of the cerebral cortex.
connective tissue
The ankle.
The fusion of the ankle bones and foot bones (the tarsus and metatarsus). Found only in some dinosaurs.
Also known as the shinbone or shankbone, is the larger, stronger, and anterior (frontal) of the two bones in the leg below the knee in vertebrates that connects the knee with the ankle bones.
The fusion of the tibia and fibula. Found in some amphibians.
Any of the digits of the foot of a tetrapod.
The middle section of the body of an insect, between the head and the abdomen, bearing the legs and wings.
The fusion of proximal elements of the tarsus and the tibia. Found only in theropod dinosaurs.
Also ichnofossil, is a fossil record of biological activity but not the preserved remains of the plant or animal itself.
The masticating organs of a rotifer including the incus and the two mallei.
The smallest and most distal wrist bone.

There are two transverse processes, one on each side of the vertebral body. They project laterally from either side at the point where the lamina joins the pedicle, between the superior and inferior articular processes.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, catalog separately. ] Trematode, no preservation information
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, prefer separate part.] See three separate parts for definition.
An abnormal benign or malignant new growth of tissue that possesses no physiological function and arises from uncontrolled usually rapid cellular proliferation— called also neoplasm.
A distal phalanx (a fingertip or toetip) which has been modified to support a nail, claw, or hoof.
Also known as the hamate. A hook shaped wrist bone.
In placental mammals, a conduit between the developing embryo or fetus and the placenta.
A liquid by-product of metabolism in humans and in many other animals.
A long unsegmented bone that represents a number of fused vertebrae and forms the posterior part of the vertebral column of frogs and toads.
A type of poison, especially one secreted by an animal.

Also mating plug, copulation plug, sperm plug, sement or sphragis. A gelatinous secretion used in the mating of some species. It is deposited by a male into a female genital tract, such as the vagina, and later hardens into a plug or glues the tract together.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, consider part=unknown and appropriate modifiers. ] An unspecified internal organ of the body.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, consider part=hair and appropriate modifiers. ] Also whiskers. A type of stiff, functional hair used by animals to sense their environment.

one of the unpaired facial bones of the skull. It is located in the midsagittal line, and articulates with the sphenoid, the ethmoid, the left and right palatine bones, and the left and right maxillary bones.
An intervertebral disc (or intervertebral fibrocartilage) lies between adjacent vertebrae in the vertebral column.
Also articular processes. Projections of the vertebra that serve the purpose of fitting with an adjacent vertebra. The actual region of contact is called the articular facet.
A porous and fibrous structural tissue found in the stems and roots of trees and other woody plants.
A bone which forms the distal ridge of the eye socket.
